description: We're a team exploring how satellite data can make farming more sustainable. Our project focuses on crop rotation, vegetation monitoring, and helping farmers make better-informed decisions using Earth observation data.
summary:
TerraCycle is a farm assistant you talk to. A farmer asks a question in plain words, such as "what should I plant on this field next year?", and gets one direct answer for that field, with the reasoning and sources one tap away.

The answer is built from NASA data. NASA POWER provides 20 years of daily weather. NASA HLS imagery, alongside 10 m Sentinel-2 images, shows how green each field is and which parts are often weaker. The crop rules come from published agronomy, such as FAO papers and Romanian field trials.

A small open language model, fine-tuned by our team and running locally, reads the question and words the answer. It is never allowed to supply a number, and when the app has no sourced value it says so.

This matters because free Earth observation data exists, but it is built for specialists. Farmers, especially those with small plots, need it turned into one sentence about their own land, and they need to know where every figure comes from.
details:
What it does

The farmer opens the app and asks a question, by typing or tapping. The assistant asks for anything it is missing (which field, what matters most: saving water, soil health or income) and answers in one sentence. The app has three screens:

  • Ask: a headline about the area's weather, fields that need a look, and the conversation.
  • My land: the fields on a satellite map, with parts that are often less green marked inside the field.
  • Data: the charts behind the answers. Each card is one large sentence that opens to its chart and is labelled "Measured on your field" or "Estimate for your area".

How it works

  • Rotation: candidate crops are first filtered by published rotation rules: years between the same crop, crops that should not follow each other, shared diseases. The remaining crops are ranked by how many of the 20 reference years (2001–2020, NASA POWER) had enough rain for each one, using FAO ECOCROP ranges. The answer is a three-year plan, and every crop left out shows the rule that excluded it.
  • Field health: we read each field on clean 10 m squares (Sentinel-2) and 30 m squares (NASA HLS) that lie fully inside its outline. Every 10 m square is compared with the rest of the same field over 10 growing seasons. The app says what the satellite sees ("less green"), never a diagnosis.
  • Sourced answers: sowing dates, years between crops, heat thresholds at flowering and soil type come from a crop table where every value records its source, page and verification status. An automated test rejects any number without a source.
  • AI: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with a LoRA adapter we trained on about 10,000 examples and 1,000 passages of specialist literature (FAO Papers 56 and 66, Fundulea field trials, reviews on heat stress). It reads the question and words the answer from the facts it is given. The server rejects any sentence that contains a number or source not in those facts. On 110 hand-written test questions, full understanding rose from 2% to 93%, and answers passing the safety check rose from 30% to 100%. It answers in about one second on a laptop GPU, and no question leaves the machine.

Benefits and impact

  • One direct answer instead of dashboards.
  • Every figure traceable to a source.
  • Small plots read at 10 m: our narrowest field is 2 ha and 71 m wide.
  • "I don't know" when there is no source.

We designed it as a public service an agriculture ministry or paying agency could run for free. The field outlines and crop history already exist in subsidy systems, and all data sources are global and free. A field's stored data is about 300 KB.

Tools

  • Code: Python (FastAPI) for the server and data pipeline; TypeScript, React Native and Expo for the phone app.
  • Data: Google Earth Engine for satellite data; Leaflet for maps; PyTorch and PEFT for fine-tuning, trained on Google Colab.

What makes it creative

  • The model words answers but cannot invent figures.
  • The app separates "measured on your field" from "estimated for your area" everywhere.
  • The satellite season curve reveals whether a winter or spring crop was grown each year.

Factors we considered and limits

  • Farmers asked for simplicity, so each answer is one sentence plus at most one visual and tap replies.
  • Small plots read at 10 m; below about 10 clean squares the app says the plot is too small to read.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: four sourced values are marked "not confirmed" in the answer.
  • Limits we state openly:
    • The crop table and sowing dates are for southern Romania. Satellite and weather readings work anywhere; we tested parcels in the USA, Argentina, India and Kenya.
    • The demo farm's crop history is sample data. Field outlines and all measurements are real.
    • There is no yield data, so recommendations are traceable, not validated.
    • The model is English-only and runs on a laptop, not the phone.
